title: Napoleon's restoration of slavery; Guadeloupe and Saint-Domingue expeditions, 1802
summary: In winter 1801–02 Napoleon Bonaparte sent expeditions to restore the Caribbean plantation order, the largest under General Leclerc to Saint-Domingue. A law of 20 May 1802 kept slavery where it had never ended, and slavery was gradually restored in Guadeloupe after Louis Delgrès's resistance. The Saint-Domingue campaign failed, leading to Haitian independence.

uncertainty.note: Saint-Domingue landings were in February 1802; the law is dated 20 May 1802; the Guadeloupe reconquest and restoration ran through 1802 (restoration there was gradual per BnF).

as_recorded.value: French troops landed simultaneously in various ports of Saint-Domingue in February 1802
1802 Battle of Matouba; slavery is reinstated in Guadeloupe

importance.justification: Reversed the 1794 abolition in much of the French Caribbean and triggered the war that ended in Haitian independence.

audience_note: Concerns the re-imposition of chattel slavery and colonial warfare, including mass deaths; no graphic detail is given here.

reviewer_note: Two theatres combined in one pin; the formal Guadeloupe restoration decrees (dated later in 1802 or 1803 in some accounts) were not confirmed on an opened page. Slavery was never formally restored in Saint-Domingue.
